cards.title: Balancing alcohol combustion: subtract the fuel's own oxygen

walkthrough.question:
Ethanol, C2H5OH, burns completely in oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water. The equation is balanced using the smallest whole numbers. What is the coefficient of O2?
A. 1
B. 2
C. 3
D. 7
walkthrough.key_idea: Balance C, then H, then O last, after subtracting the fuel's own O.
walkthrough.careful: Subtract the oxygen atom already inside the alcohol.
procedure: Write fuel + O2 → CO2 + H2O.
Balance C: number of CO2 equals number of carbons.
Balance H: number of H2O is half the hydrogens.
Count O on the right; subtract the fuel's O.
Halve the remainder for O2; double everything if fractional.
tricks: Saturated alcohol CnH2n+1OH needs 3n/2 O2. Fails for rings or C=C.
Check: product O atoms = fuel O + 2 × O2 coefficient.
if_lost: What are the two products of complete combustion?
How many CO2 molecules do two carbon atoms make?
How many water molecules hold six hydrogen atoms?
How many oxygen atoms does ethanol bring by itself?

1_context.short: AO2: write a combustion equation for an alcohol.
1_context.why: The R1.3.1 skill names alcohols specifically. The oxygen already in the fuel is the twist examiners use to separate students who balance mechanically.
1_context.avoid: Treating ethanol like a hydrocarbon and ignoring the O in OH.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.3.1: deduce equations for combustion reactions, including hydrocarbons and alcohols.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books mostly practise alkanes. The exam swaps in an alcohol, which changes the oxygen count.

2_markscheme_logic.short: One mark for the letter: only C (3) scores.
2_markscheme_logic.why: MCQs are all or nothing. Each distractor is the number you get from one slip in the oxygen count.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Choosing D: the most common error was not counting ethanol's oxygen atom (25M.1A.SL.TZ2.17).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: 7 comes from supplying all 7 product O atoms from O2. It ignores ethanol's own O.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Right: 4 + 3 = 7 O atoms on the right, minus 1 from ethanol = 6, so 3 O2. Tempting: all 7 from O2.

3_novel_application.short: Any fuel containing O: subtract its oxygen before halving.
3_novel_application.why: The method is the same for ethers, sugars or fuels containing Pb or S. Each extra element needs its own oxide product, then the O count is done last.
3_novel_application.avoid: Leaving out a product for an extra element, such as PbO2 from PbC8H20 (12M.2.SL.TZ1.2).
3_novel_application.disguise: The fuel contains O (an alcohol or ether) or another element (S, Pb) that also takes oxygen.
3_novel_application.heuristic: List every element in the fuel. Each one needs a product, and the fuel's O counts on the left.

4_command_terms.short: No command term: one mark for the correct letter.
4_command_terms.why: No working is marked. Write the balance quickly in the margin and read off one coefficient.
4_command_terms.avoid: Picking the first option that matches a count you made halfway through.
4_command_terms.demands: Balance the whole equation, then report the O2 coefficient.

5_time_efficiency.short: C, then H, then O last: under 40 seconds.
5_time_efficiency.why: C and H each sit in only one product, so they set the right side. Oxygen appears everywhere, so it is balanced last.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Starting with oxygen, which forces you to redo every coefficient.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No doubling needed: ethanol already gives whole numbers.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 14 gives alcohol formulas if only a name appears.
6_data_booklet.why: Section 14 lists propan-1-ol C3H7OH and butan-1-ol C4H9OH with states, which saves deriving formulas from names.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking for combustion products or balancing rules in the booklet.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 14 table: formula column for alcohols such as C3H7OH and C4H9OH.
6_data_booklet.memorise: The products of complete combustion (CO2, H2O) and how to balance are NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: A is too small for two carbons; D is a count of atoms.
7_elimination.why: Two carbons need 4 O atoms just for the CO2. One O2 gives only 2, so A fails before you even count water.
7_elimination.avoid: Picking D because 7 appears in your working.

definitely_wrong.rule: One O2 cannot even supply the oxygen for 2 CO2.
7 is the product O-atom total. It ignores ethanol's O and is atoms, not molecules.

walkthrough.answer: C. C2H5OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O: 7 product O atoms minus ethanol's 1 leaves 6, which is 3 O2.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.3.1: deduce equations for combustion of hydrocarbons and alcohols.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books drill alkanes. Exams use alcohols, larger alkanes (nonane, octane) or fuels with other elements.

trigger_phrases: fully balanced equation with CO2 and H2O
per 1 mol of fuel (fractional O2 allowed)
trap_boundaries: Ignoring the alcohol's O gives the D distractor (25M.1A.SL.TZ2.17).
Fuels with Pb need PbO2 as a product (12M.2.SL.TZ1.2).
If combustion gives only CO2 and H2O, the compound cannot contain N (24M.2.SL.TZ2.1).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial understanding balances C and H correctly. Full credit needs the O count to include the fuel's oxygen.

disguises: Sum of coefficients for 1 mol of propan-1-ol (fractional O2: 4.5)
Octane burning with 12.5 O2 (19M.2.SL.TZ1.13)
Organometallic or sulfur-containing fuels
3_novel_application.heuristic: Every element in the fuel goes to its oxide. Oxygen is balanced last, after crediting the fuel's own O.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: In MCQs 1 mark for the letter. In Paper 2 the equation usually scores 1 mark for correct formulas and balancing.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Don't write state symbols or double coefficients unless the stem asks for whole numbers.

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 14 gives formulas for propan-1-ol, butan-1-ol, cyclohexanol and phenol. Balancing itself is NOT in the booklet.

rules: An O2 coefficient smaller than the number of carbons is impossible for complete combustion.
If an option equals the total of product O atoms, it ignores the fuel's O.
Products only CO2 and H2O mean no N is present (24M.2.SL.TZ2.1).

evidence.note: Ethanol complete combustion, O2 coefficient 3; 77% correct.
Most common mistake: ignoring ethanol's O atom, leading to D.
Sum of coefficients for 1 mol propan-1-ol is 12.5.
Credits C2H5OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O.
Octane needs 12.5 O2 per mole; ethanol 3 O2.
Weaker candidates left out PbO2 or O2 when balancing PbC8H20 combustion.
N–H was chosen even though the only combustion products were CO2 and H2O.

cards.difficulty_signal: 77% correct on 25M SL (D the main distractor). 'Balanced equation' is a repeated error signal in reports.

cards.title: Combustion stoichiometry: write the equation the stem doesn't give

walkthrough.question:
Propane, C3H8 (Mr = 44.1 g mol−1), is burned completely. How many moles of oxygen are needed for 11.5 g of propane?
A. 10.4
B. 5.20
C. 2.60
D. 1.30
walkthrough.key_idea: Moles of fuel × O2-to-fuel ratio from your own balanced equation.
walkthrough.careful: Use the O2 ratio for one mole of fuel.
procedure: Write and balance the complete combustion equation.
Convert the mass of fuel to moles: n = m/M.
Multiply by the O2 : fuel mole ratio.
Round to the significant figures of the data.
tricks: Alkane CnH2n+2 needs (3n+1)/2 O2 per mole. Alkanes only.
Gases at same T and p: volumes follow coefficients. Fails for liquids or solids.
Options doubling each other point to a ratio slip. Recheck the coefficient per fuel.
if_lost: What does propane form when it burns completely?
How many O2 does one propane need in the balanced equation?
How do you turn 11.5 g into moles?

1_context.short: AO2: combine a combustion equation with a mole calculation.
1_context.why: The stem gives no equation. You must deduce it and then use it, which is two skills chained together. That is why it discriminates well.
1_context.avoid: Guessing a ratio without writing the balanced equation.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.3.1: deduce equations for combustion of hydrocarbons.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books balance equations and do moles in separate chapters. This question needs both at once.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Only D (1.30) scores; others are doubling slips.
2_markscheme_logic.why: 0.261 mol × 5 = 1.30. The distractors are 0.261 × 10, × 20 and × 40, so each one is a coefficient error.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Skipping the equation: the examiner called this an excellent discriminator (about 65% correct, 25M.1A.HL.6219.30).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Using the O2 coefficient from 2C3H8 + 10O2 for one propane gives 2.60, which is wrong.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Right: 5 O2 per C3H8. Tempting: 10 O2, the coefficient from the doubled equation.

3_novel_application.short: Asked for CO2, SO2 or a volume: still ratio × moles.
3_novel_application.why: Every variant is the same chain: the fuel amount goes through the equation ratio to the amount wanted. Only the start and end units change.
3_novel_application.avoid: Using molar volume when volumes can be compared directly by coefficients (25M.1A.HL.6219.3).
3_novel_application.disguise: CO2 per gram of ethanol vs octane (19M.2.SL.TZ1.13), SO2 from sulfur in coal (22N.2.SL.TZ0.5), or a gas volume of butane.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Find the fuel's amount, find the ratio in the equation, scale. Then convert units only at the end.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ: no working marked, one mark.
4_command_terms.why: Since only the letter counts, write the equation and the ratio quickly and check the options against your estimate.
4_command_terms.avoid: Doing a long calculation before ruling out impossible options.
4_command_terms.demands: Deduce the equation, then the amount of O2.

5_time_efficiency.why: 11.5 is about a quarter of 44.1, and a quarter times 5 is about 1.3. Estimating picks the option without a calculator.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Working out the mass of O2: the question asks for moles.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip the CO2 and water amounts and the O2 mass.

6_data_booklet.short: The booklet doesn't help; Mr is in the stem.
6_data_booklet.why: Everything needed is in the stem or the equation you write. The booklet adds nothing here.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Combustion equations and mole ratios are NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Over 2 mol O2 for a quarter mole of propane: impossible.
7_elimination.why: No small hydrocarbon needs 10 or more O2 per molecule. Options at 10× or more of the fuel amount break chemistry.
7_elimination.avoid: Trusting an option just because it is a neat multiple of your mole value.

definitely_wrong.rule: Needs 40 O2 per propane: absurd for a C3 fuel.
Needs 20 O2 per propane: absurd.
10 O2 per propane is the doubled-equation coefficient applied to one molecule.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.3.1 combustion equations; R1.3.3: evaluate the CO2 added when different fuels burn.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books leave 'CO2 per gram of fuel' to discussion. Exams make it a calculation comparing fuels (ethanol vs octane).

trap_boundaries: A wrong O2 coefficient leads to a doubled distractor.
When comparing fuels, compare equal masses: 1 g ethanol gives about 0.04 mol CO2, 1 g octane about 0.07 mol (19M.2.SL.TZ1.13).
Sulfur to SO2 is 1:1 by moles (22N.2.SL.TZ0.5).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial credit: the right equation but per-mole comparison. Full credit: per gram of fuel, as the markscheme does.

disguises: Volume of butane to make 40 cm3 CO2
Which fuel adds more CO2 per gram
Moles of SO2 from % sulfur in coal
3_novel_application.heuristic: Fuel amount × equation ratio = product amount. Convert units only at the start and end.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Paper 2 calculations give 1 mark per stage (e.g. mass of S, then mol SO2), with a correct final answer usually earning all of them.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: For same-T,p gas volumes skip moles entirely: scale by coefficients.

6_data_booklet.hack: Nothing to look up: combustion equations and mole ratios are NOT in the booklet, and Mr is normally given.

rules: An O2 requirement many times the fuel amount is impossible for small fuels.
A fuel with more C per gram (hydrocarbon vs alcohol) gives more CO2 per gram.
For gas volumes, the answer is a simple coefficient ratio of the given volume.

evidence.note: 11.5 g propane needs 1.30 mol O2; about 65% correct, 'excellent discriminator'.
Butane volume from CO2 volume by coefficients; over 80% correct.
CO2 per gram: ethanol 0.04 mol vs octane 0.07 mol; octane produces more.
0.40% S in 500.0 g gives 2.0 g, 0.062 mol S, 0.062 mol SO2.

cards.difficulty_signal: About 65% on 25M 6219.30 (excellent discriminator). Reports list CO2-from-fuel calculations as difficult (Nov 2017).

cards.title: Incomplete combustion: hydrogen always ends as water, never H2

walkthrough.question:
Propane burns with too little oxygen (incomplete combustion). Which products may form?
A. CO2 and H2 only
B. CO, C and H2
C. CO2, H2O and H2
D. CO2, CO and C
walkthrough.key_idea: H always becomes water; carbon splits between CO2, CO and soot.
walkthrough.careful: Never list H2 as a combustion product.
procedure: Note the fuel's elements: carbon and hydrogen.
Hydrogen is always oxidised to H2O.
With limited oxygen, carbon gives CO2, CO or C.
Reject any option that contains H2.
tricks: Any option with H2 is wrong for combustion.
Soot and CO can form together with some CO2 in one flame.
if_lost: Where do hydrogen atoms end up when anything burns?
What can carbon form if oxygen runs short?
Which options contain a product that never forms in combustion?

1_context.short: AO1: recall the products of incomplete combustion.
1_context.why: R1.3.2 names carbon monoxide and carbon. Exams test it by offering hydrogen as a tempting extra product.
1_context.avoid: Thinking 'incomplete' means the fuel splits back into its elements, including H2.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.3.2: incomplete combustion of organic compounds gives carbon monoxide and carbon.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show one tidy equation making CO. Exams mix CO2, CO and C, and add H2 as bait.

2_markscheme_logic.short: D only: CO2, CO and C can all appear.
2_markscheme_logic.why: 'May form' means any product that is possible. In limited oxygen all three carbon products are possible, and water always forms.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Choosing an H2 option: 31% thought H2 and CO2 form (16N.1.HL.TZ0.27); same error in 24M.1.SL.TZ1.27.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: H2 is never credited. Naming 'incomplete combustion' as a condition doesn't answer a products question (14M.2.SL.TZ2.3).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Right: every H goes to H2O. Tempting: H2 listed as a product.

3_novel_application.short: Soot on glassware or a yellow flame means incomplete combustion.
3_novel_application.why: A practical question may never say 'incomplete combustion'. A black deposit from a closed air hole is carbon, and it changes the mass readings (16N.3.SL.TZ0.2).
3_novel_application.avoid: Blaming soot on the crucible burning (16N.3.HL.TZ0.2).
3_novel_application.disguise: Soot on a crucible during heating, 'limited air' wording, or burning plastics.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Black deposit or smoky flame: carbon from too little oxygen.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ: pick everything that could form.
4_command_terms.why: The 12N report noted that 'could' and 'limited oxygen' wording tripped many students. Read the stem for possibility, not certainty (12N.1.SL.TZ0.29).
4_command_terms.avoid: Rejecting D because CO2 also forms in complete combustion.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the set of products that may form.

5_time_efficiency.short: Cross out every H2 option: done in 10 seconds.
5_time_efficiency.why: Three of the four options contain H2. One rule removes them without any balancing.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Writing and balancing incomplete-combustion equations for each option.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No balancing: this is recognising products.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 14: CO and C still have energy to release.
6_data_booklet.why: CO (−283) and carbon (−394) both have combustion enthalpies in section 14. Making them instead of CO2 wastes the fuel's energy.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Thinking the booklet lists incomplete combustion products.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 14 rows for CO(g) −283 and C(graphite) −394 kJ mol−1.
6_data_booklet.memorise: The products of incomplete combustion are NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: A, B and C all contain H2.
7_elimination.why: Hydrogen in a fuel is oxidised to water even when oxygen is scarce, so H2 is never a combustion product.
7_elimination.avoid: Keeping C because it also has water.

definitely_wrong.rule: Contains H2.
Contains H2.
Contains H2.

walkthrough.answer: D. With limited oxygen, carbon may form CO2, CO and C (soot). Hydrogen forms water, never H2.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.3.2: incomplete combustion gives CO and C; deduce equations for hydrocarbons and alcohols.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show CO alone. Exams use mixed products, practical soot and H2 distractors.

trap_boundaries: H2 as a product is wrong (24M.1.SL.TZ1.27, 16N.1.HL.TZ0.27).
Answering with a condition when products are asked (14M.2.SL.TZ2.3).
Soot lowers the measured result in a crucible experiment (16N.3.SL.TZ0.2).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial: names CO only. Full: CO and/or C as the markscheme lists, with all H as water.

disguises: Soot deposited on a crucible
'Limited supply of oxygen' vs 'incomplete combustion' wording
Combustion of PVC or other polymers
3_novel_application.heuristic: Look for a black deposit or yellow flame. Carbon has not fully oxidised, but hydrogen always becomes water.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: 'State' a product: 1 mark (CO or C/soot both accepted in 21M.2.SL.TZ1.5). An equation must be balanced.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No balancing needed for product-recognition MCQs.

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 14 gives ΔHc for CO (−283) and C (−394): incomplete combustion leaves this energy unreleased. The products themselves are NOT in the booklet.

rules: Any option containing H2 is wrong.
An option with only CO2 and H2O describes complete combustion.
No N-containing product can form from a C/H/O fuel.

evidence.note: Propane incomplete combustion: CO2, CO and C.
(c) credits carbon monoxide/CO or carbon/C/soot.
59% correct; 31% thought H2 and CO2 would form.
Candidates thought hydrogen would be a product of incomplete combustion.
Hardest question on the paper; 'could' and limited-oxygen wording misread.
(b) soot/carbon deposited, incomplete combustion, air hole not open.
Some gave hydrogen as a product or stated a condition instead.

cards.difficulty_signal: 59% correct on 16N with 31% choosing H2. 12N was the hardest item on its paper; H2 misconception again in 24M.

cards.title: Fossil fuel impacts: match each pollutant to its effect

walkthrough.question:
Which statement describes an environmental effect of burning fossil fuels?
A. Greater biodiversity because mining creates new habitats
B. Lower greenhouse gas emissions, leading to global cooling
C. More fertile soil because coal dust settles on it
D. Acid rain from released sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides
walkthrough.key_idea: Fossil fuels release CO2 (warming) and SO2/NOx (acid rain).
walkthrough.careful: CO2 means warming; SO2 and NOx mean acid rain.
procedure: List what burning a fossil fuel releases.
CO2 absorbs infrared from Earth: enhanced greenhouse effect.
Sulfur impurities give SO2; hot engines give NOx.
SO2 and NOx dissolve in rain to form acids.
Choose the option pairing a real emission with its effect.
tricks: Options claiming fossil fuels benefit the environment are wrong.
Acid rain is SO2/NOx. CO2 alone is a greenhouse and ocean issue.
if_lost: What gases leave a coal power station chimney?
Which of those gases form acids with water?
Does burning fossil fuels raise or lower greenhouse gases?

1_context.short: AO1: know the disadvantages of fossil fuels.
1_context.why: R1.3.3 asks for advantages and disadvantages of fossil fuels and the CO2–greenhouse link. Examiners pair each pollutant with one effect.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.3.3: fossil fuels have advantages and disadvantages; link CO2 levels to the greenhouse effect.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books list impacts loosely. Exams reward precise pollutant–effect pairs and penalise mix-ups.

2_markscheme_logic.short: D: SO2 and NOx cause acid rain.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Sulfur in coal and oil burns to SO2, and nitrogen oxides form in hot combustion. Both give acids in rainwater.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Treating the greenhouse effect as ozone depletion (14M.3.SL.TZ1.14).
trigger_phrases: CO2 absorbs IR re-radiated from Earth
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Right: a real emission with its real effect. Distractors claim a benefit or a decrease.

3_novel_application.short: A coal sulfur % question is the same idea with numbers.
3_novel_application.why: 22N.2.SL.TZ0.5 turns it into mass of S to mol SO2, an acid rain equation (SO2 + H2O → H2SO3), and fixes such as removing sulfur or adding lime.
3_novel_application.avoid: Writing H2CO3 when asked how SO2 forms acid rain.
3_novel_application.disguise: Coal with % sulfur, greenhouse gas lists, or ways to reduce CO2 emissions.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Sulfur leads to SO2 and acid. Carbon leads to CO2, IR absorption and warming.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ: one mark for the single correct pair.
4_command_terms.why: Only one option names both a real emission and a real effect. The others are statements that are simply false.
4_command_terms.demands: Recognise a correct pollutant and effect pair.

5_time_efficiency.short: Find the named gas; check its effect: 15 seconds.
5_time_efficiency.why: Only one option names an emitted gas. Checking it against its known effect settles the question.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Ignore mining and habitat arguments: they are not chemistry of combustion.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 14 lists sulfur: it burns like a fuel.
6_data_booklet.why: Section 14 gives sulfur's ΔHc (−297 kJ mol−1). Sulfur impurities burn alongside the fuel, which is where SO2 comes from.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Expecting greenhouse gases or acid rain equations in the booklet.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 14 row: sulfur S(s), −297 kJ mol−1.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Greenhouse gases, the IR mechanism and acid rain equations are NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: A, B and C claim benefits from fossil fuels.
7_elimination.why: Burning fossil fuels adds greenhouse gases and pollutants. Any option describing an improvement can go without further thought.
7_elimination.avoid: Keeping C because coal contains minerals.

definitely_wrong.rule: Mining destroys habitats; it doesn't raise biodiversity.
Fossil fuels increase greenhouse gases; they never cause cooling by lowering them.
Coal dust is particulate pollution, not fertiliser.

walkthrough.answer: D. Sulfur impurities burn to SO2 and hot combustion makes NOx. Both dissolve in rain to form acid rain.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.3.3: fossil fuels' advantages and disadvantages; CO2 and the greenhouse effect.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books describe impacts in prose. Exams ask for precise mechanisms (IR from Earth) and equations (SO2 to acid).

trigger_phrases: absorbs infrared radiation re-radiated by Earth
methane more potent, CO2 more abundant
trap_boundaries: CO2 linked to acid rain is a misconception (16N.3.SL.TZ0.13).
Ozone or UV talk in a greenhouse answer doesn't score (14M.3.SL.TZ1.14).
Writing NO2 for N2O as a greenhouse gas is wrong (18M.3.HL.TZ1.11).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial: names the gas. Full: names the gas and its mechanism or equation.

disguises: % sulfur in coal to mol SO2 (22N.2.SL.TZ0.5)
Evidence linking CO2 to temperature (19N.3.SL.TZ0.14)
Methane vs CO2 as greenhouse gases (20N.2.SL.TZ0.11)
3_novel_application.heuristic: Trace each element of the fuel to its oxide, then to that oxide's effect.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark per valid point. Suggest-type questions accept any listed method, e.g. scrubbers, carbon capture, alternative energy (19M.2.SL.TZ2.13).

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip journalistic background. One specific mechanism per mark.

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 14 lists sulfur's ΔHc (−297), a reminder that S burns to SO2. Greenhouse and acid rain chemistry is NOT in the booklet.

rules: Fossil fuels never lower greenhouse emissions or cool the planet.
Acid rain answers must involve SO2 or NOx, not CO2 alone.
Greenhouse answers mention IR, not UV or ozone.

evidence.note: Acid rain from SO2 and NOx is the environmental effect of fossil fuels.
S mass to 0.062 mol SO2; SO2 + H2O → H2SO3; remove S or add lime.
Greenhouse gases list and ways to reduce CO2.
Greenhouse effect confused with ozone; IR from Earth, not Sun, often missed.
Candidates wrongly related CO2 to acid rain.
(e) CO2 more abundant; methane more potent IR absorber.

cards.difficulty_signal: The MCQ has no % data. Reports repeatedly flag the greenhouse mechanism and CO2/acid rain confusion.

cards.title: Photosynthesis equation: the carbon fixation behind biofuels

walkthrough.question: Ethanol biofuel is made from glucose, which plants produce by photosynthesis (biological fixation of carbon). Part (a): state the balanced equation for photosynthesis. [1]
walkthrough.careful: Products are glucose AND oxygen; don't write respiration.
procedure: Reactants: carbon dioxide and water.
Products: glucose C6H12O6 and oxygen.
Balance C with 6 CO2 and H with 6 H2O.
Check O: 18 on each side, so 6 O2.
tricks: Every coefficient is 6 except glucose's 1.
Flip glucose combustion: if that balances, this does too.
if_lost: Which gas do plants take in from the air?
What is the molecular formula of glucose?
Which gas do plants give out in light?

1_context.short: AO1: recall a balanced equation named in the guidance.
1_context.why: R1.3.4 guidance says the reactants and products of photosynthesis should be known. That makes it a recall mark many students lose.
1_context.avoid: Assuming it's biology-only and not revising it.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.3.4: biofuels come from carbon fixed by photosynthesis; its reactants and products should be known.
1_context.textbook_gap: Biology teaches it in words. Chemistry wants a balanced equation with the correct glucose formula.

2_markscheme_logic.short: One mark for the full balanced equation.
2_markscheme_logic.why: There is no partial credit: one wrong formula or coefficient loses the only mark.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Unbalanced equation, missing O2, reverse reaction or wrong glucose formula: all reported (25M.2.HL.6221.9).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Respiration (glucose + O2 → CO2 + H2O) scores zero.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Zero vs one mark: every species present and every 6 in place.

3_novel_application.short: 'Why is a biofuel carbon neutral?' uses this equation.
3_novel_application.why: 19N.3.SL.TZ0.14 credits saying the biofuel's raw material used up CO2 when it formed, with this equation. Burning returns that CO2.
3_novel_application.avoid: Saying biofuels release no CO2 when burned.
3_novel_application.disguise: Asked how biofuels reduce net CO2, or what 'biological fixation of carbon' means.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Biofuel carbon came from the air through photosynthesis, so burning only returns it.

4_command_terms.why: 'State' wants a brief specific answer. Writing words around the equation earns nothing extra.

5_time_efficiency.short: Write it from memory in 20 seconds.
5_time_efficiency.why: This is recall: no derivation is needed, and the 18-oxygen check takes seconds.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: State symbols are optional extras here; no explanation needed.

6_data_booklet.short: Nothing in the booklet: learn it.
6_data_booklet.why: The booklet has no biochemical equations, so the only route is memory.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Wasting time searching sections for glucose.
6_data_booklet.memorise: The photosynthesis equation and glucose formula C6H12O6 are NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: O2 on the left means you wrote respiration.
7_elimination.why: Photosynthesis releases oxygen. If O2 is a reactant, you have written cellular respiration, which examiners saw often.
7_elimination.avoid: Leaving O2 out to make balancing easier.

definitely_wrong.target: An equation with O2 as a reactant
definitely_wrong.rule: That is respiration, not photosynthesis.
The oxygen atoms cannot balance without O2 as a product.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.3.4: biofuels from carbon fixed by photosynthesis; know its reactants and products.
1_context.textbook_gap: Usually taught in biology. The chemistry exam asks for the balanced symbol equation and uses it to explain carbon neutrality.

trigger_phrases: raw material uses up CO2 during its formation
trap_boundaries: Reverse reaction (respiration), missing O2, wrong glucose formula or unbalanced: 0 marks (25M.2.HL.6221.9).
Crops absorb CO2 as they grow: few gave this to explain biofuel carbon (18M.3.SL.TZ1.11).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A single mark: only the complete balanced equation earns it.

disguises: Why biofuels are carbon neutral
'Biological fixation of carbon' in the stem
Fermentation of glucose to ethanol as the next step
3_novel_application.heuristic: Biofuel carbon was taken from the air by photosynthesis, so burning returns it.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: 'State' the equation: 1 mark. 'Explain' carbon neutrality: separate marks for CO2 uptake and the equation (19N.3.SL.TZ0.14).

6_data_booklet.hack: Nothing to look up: the photosynthesis equation is NOT in the booklet and must be memorised.

rules: O2 as a reactant means respiration, which is wrong.
Glucose is C6H12O6; any other formula fails.
All coefficients except glucose's are 6.

evidence.note: Half stated it; errors were unbalanced equations, missing O2, respiration given, wrong glucose formula.
A surprising number did not know the photosynthesis equation.
(c) biofuel raw material uses up CO2; photosynthesis equation credited.
Few explained that biofuel crops absorb CO2 as they grow.

cards.difficulty_signal: Only about half scored it in 25M HL (the question overall was 40%). Flagged again in 25M SL TZ3.

cards.title: Biofuel pros and cons: name the chemical, compare with the fossil fuel

walkthrough.question: Ethanol from crops can be used in place of gasoline (petrol). Part (b)(i): outline two advantages of ethanol over gasoline as a fuel. [2]
walkthrough.key_idea: Two distinct, specific points: renewable; less net CO2; less SO2 or CO.
walkthrough.careful: 'Less harmful' alone scores nothing: name the effect.
procedure: Pick two different categories: source, carbon, pollutants.
Source: renewable or sustainable, regrown quickly.
Carbon: crops absorb CO2, lower carbon footprint.
Pollutants: less SO2 (acid rain) or less CO/soot.
Phrase each point as a comparison with gasoline.
tricks: One mark per distinct idea: don't give two versions of 'green'.
For disadvantages think land: food crops, deforestation, fertilisers.
if_lost: How quickly is each fuel's source replaced?
Where did the carbon in the crop come from?
Which fossil-fuel pollutant comes from an impurity?

1_context.short: AO2: outline biofuel advantages against a fossil fuel.
1_context.why: R1.3.4 asks you to weigh biofuels against fossil fuels. The question rewards chemistry-based reasons, not general opinions.
1_context.avoid: Giving general 'better for the planet' answers.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.3.4: advantages and disadvantages of biofuels; renewable vs non-renewable sources.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books give long pros and cons lists. Marks go only to precise, comparative points.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Two different credited ideas, 1 mark each, 2 max.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The markscheme lists renewable, lower CO2 footprint, less SO2/acid rain and less CO/soot. Biodegradable or less toxic is also accepted.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Vague answers: reports noted weak global-impact reasoning (25M.2.SL.TZ3.8).
trigger_phrases: low or zero carbon footprint / less CO2
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Just 'less harmful' is not accepted; 2 max.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial: one idea or two versions of it. Full: two different ideas, each a named effect.

3_novel_application.short: 'Production' questions want land use, not combustion.
3_novel_application.why: In 19M.3.SL.TZ1.13 many answered about burning biodiesel when asked about producing it. About a third gave land area, the credited idea.
3_novel_application.avoid: Answering about combustion when the stem says production.
3_novel_application.disguise: A disadvantage MCQ, biodiesel instead of ethanol, or 'production from renewable resources'.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Split the life cycle: growing (land, food, fertiliser) vs burning (CO2, SO2, CO).

4_command_terms.why: 'Outline' wants a brief account. Two clear lines, each a distinct advantage, fit the two marks exactly.
4_command_terms.avoid: Writing a paragraph that blends two ideas into one.
4_command_terms.demands: Two brief advantages, each compared with gasoline.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: 1 mark per distinct valid advantage, max 2.

5_time_efficiency.short: Two lines, two categories: under a minute.
5_time_efficiency.why: Choosing from different categories guarantees the points are distinct, so neither mark is lost to repetition.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Listing four points: the extra ones earn nothing.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No explanation of photosynthesis unless asked; one line per point.

6_data_booklet.short: The booklet has no biofuel pros and cons.
6_data_booklet.why: This is evaluation knowledge. No table lists it, so prepared categories are your shortcut.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Biofuel advantages and disadvantages are NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.why: Ethanol is already partly oxidised, so it releases less energy per gram than fossil hydrocarbons (17M.3.HL.TZ2.17). 'Releases more energy' cannot be an advantage.

definitely_wrong.rule: Not accepted: name the pollutant or the carbon cycle.
Fossil fuels have higher specific energy than biofuels.

walkthrough.answer: Any two [2 max]: renewable/sustainable; lower carbon footprint/less CO2; less SO2/less acid rain; less incomplete combustion (less CO/soot). Biodegradable/less toxic is also accepted; 'less harmful' alone is not.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.3.4: advantages and disadvantages of biofuels; renewable vs non-renewable.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books give opinion-style lists. Exams credit only specific, comparative chemistry points.

trap_boundaries: 'Less harmful' alone is rejected (25M.2.HL.6221.9).
Answering combustion when production is asked (19M.3.SL.TZ1.13).
Listing the same idea twice earns one mark.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial: one specific idea. Full: two distinct ideas, each naming a chemical or process.

disguises: Disadvantage MCQ: land that could grow food
Biodiesel pros and cons (20N.2.SL.TZ0.11)
Ethanol vs octane CO2 per gram (19M.2.SL.TZ1.13)
3_novel_application.heuristic: Split growing from burning, and compare each with the fossil fuel.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: 1 mark per distinct point. 'Compare' needs both items in every point (14M.3.SL.TZ2.8); pick one side of each contrast, not both (14N.3.SL.TZ0.10).

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Give exactly as many points as marks.

6_data_booklet.hack: Nothing to look up: biofuel pros and cons are NOT in the booklet.

rules: 'More energy per mol or per gram' is not a biofuel advantage.
'Lower CO2 emissions' is an advantage, not a disadvantage.
Land use, deforestation and food competition are disadvantages.

evidence.note: (b)(i) renewable; low carbon footprint; less SO2/acid rain; less CO/soot; 'less harmful' not accepted; 2 max.
Most scored renewability; many gained a second mark for less CO2.
Disadvantage of biofuels: land that could grow food.
(c) biodiesel advantages and disadvantages: land, deforestation, fertilisers, viscosity.
Answered combustion instead of production; land area was the credited idea.
Fossil fuels have higher specific energy than biofuels.

cards.difficulty_signal: Generally well treated (25M HL). Specific vague-answer traps still cost marks; the production vs combustion confusion was reported.

cards.title: Combustion enthalpy from bond enthalpies: count every bond, broken minus formed

walkthrough.question:
Part (b)(ii): calculate the enthalpy change of combustion of ethanol, in kJ mol−1, using average bond enthalpies (data booklet section 12).
C2H5OH(l) + 3O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 3H2O(g)
Bond enthalpies / kJ mol−1: C–C 346, C–H 414, C–O 358, O–H 463, O=O 498, C=O 804. [3]
walkthrough.key_idea: ΔH = bonds broken − bonds formed; count bonds, not atoms.
walkthrough.question_type: Bond enthalpies: combustion enthalpy of a fuel
walkthrough.careful: Broken minus formed, never formed minus broken.
procedure: Draw ethanol and list each bond with its count.
Sum bonds broken, including 3 O=O.
Sum bonds formed: 4 C=O and 6 O–H.
ΔH = broken − formed; keep the sign.
tricks: Combustion is exothermic: a positive answer means you subtracted backwards.
Ethanol has 5 C–H, not 6: one H sits on oxygen.
if_lost: Which bonds does ethanol's full structure contain?
How many O=O bonds break per ethanol?
Which bonds form in 2 CO2 and 3 H2O?

1_context.short: AO2: bond enthalpy calculation applied to a fuel.
1_context.why: R1.3 sets the bond enthalpy method from R1.2 on a fuel. A molecule with five different bond types tests careful counting.
1_context.avoid: Using molecular formula C2H6O instead of the structure.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.3.1: combustion of organic compounds; enthalpy here by the R1.2 bond enthalpy method.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books use small molecules. The exam uses a fuel with C–O and O–H, and water as gas.

2_markscheme_logic.why: Marks go to the broken sum, the formed sum and the final value. A correct final answer alone earns all three.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Subtracting the wrong way round (25M.2.HL.6221.9 examiner).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Award [3] for the correct final answer. +1263 has the wrong sign and loses the final mark.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial: correct sums but wrong order or sign. Full: −1263 kJ mol−1.

3_novel_application.short: Any fuel: draw its structure before counting.
3_novel_application.why: Bond enthalpies are averages for gases, so −1263 differs from the measured −1367 used later in the question. Expect a 'why different' follow-up.
3_novel_application.avoid: Assuming the bond-enthalpy value should match section 14.
3_novel_application.disguise: A different fuel, or energy per gram of ethanol vs octane (09M.2.SL.TZ2.6).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Structure first, then a table of bond counts. Molecular formulas hide C–O and O–H.

4_command_terms.short: 'Calculate': show the stages; final answer can carry all.
4_command_terms.why: 'Calculate' needs working. If the final number is wrong, the shown broken and formed sums still earn marks.
4_command_terms.avoid: Writing only a final number with no sums.
4_command_terms.demands: A numerical ΔH with working shown.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: 3 marks: bonds broken, bonds formed, final ΔH. A correct final answer scores 3.

5_time_efficiency.short: Bond table, two sums, one subtraction: 2 minutes.
5_time_efficiency.why: A small table of bond, count and value prevents missed bonds. It also gives the examiner your working marks.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Breaking the CO2 and H2O bonds as well.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Don't convert to kJ g−1 or compare with section 14 unless asked.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 12, as the question directs, gives the bond values.
6_data_booklet.why: The question points to section 12 for average bond enthalpies. Use the C=O value given for CO2 (804).
6_data_booklet.avoid: Using the C=O value meant for another type of compound.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 12 bond enthalpy table (as directed by the question).
6_data_booklet.memorise: Ethanol's structure and bond counts are NOT in the booklet; learn 'broken minus formed'.

7_elimination.short: Positive ΔH for combustion is wrong.
7_elimination.why: Burning a fuel always releases energy, so any positive value shows a subtraction or counting error.
7_elimination.avoid: Keeping +1263 because the arithmetic looks clean.

definitely_wrong.rule: Combustion is always exothermic.
Ethanol has only 5 C–H; the sixth H is on O.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.3.1 combustion equations, used with R1.2 bond enthalpies.
1_context.textbook_gap: Exams embed the bond enthalpy method in a biofuel context and expect the full structural bond count.

trigger_phrases: negative final value with kJ mol−1
trap_boundaries: Correct final answer: [3] (25M.2.HL.6221.9).
Wrong subtraction order loses the final mark.
A later part allows the (b)(ii) value without penalty (ECF).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial: sums right, sign or order wrong. Full: −1263 kJ mol−1.

disguises: Different fuels (alcohols, alkanes)
Energy per gram comparison (09M.2.SL.TZ2.6)
Why bond-enthalpy ΔH differs from measured ΔHc
3_novel_application.heuristic: Draw the full structure; bonds, not atoms, decide the sums.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Calculate: marks per stage, full marks for the correct final answer. Explain the difference: averages and gaseous states.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip product bonds on the 'broken' side; skip unit conversions not asked.

6_data_booklet.hack: The question directs you to section 12 for bond enthalpies. Ethanol's bond counts and the 'broken − formed' rule must be known.

rules: A positive ΔH for combustion is wrong.
A total with 6 C–H for ethanol is wrong.
Bond-enthalpy ΔH won't equal the measured ΔHc exactly.

evidence.note: (b)(ii) 4731 broken, 5994 formed, −1263 kJ mol−1; [3] for correct final answer.
About 40% got full marks; some subtracted the wrong way round.
Ethanol combustion via bond enthalpies mostly correct; energy per gram vs octane harder.

cards.difficulty_signal: About 40% full marks on 25M HL (b)(ii), the hardest R1.3 item in macro data (40% correct).

cards.title: Energy from a mass of fuel: n × |ΔHc|, then into the water

walkthrough.question:
Ethanol has Mr = 46.0 and ΔHc = −1367 kJ mol−1. Which expression gives the mass of ethanol, in g, that releases 683.5 kJ on complete combustion?
A. 683.5 / (1367 × 46.0)
B. 1367 / (683.5 × 46.0)
C. (683.5 × 46.0) / 1367
D. (1367 × 46.0) / 683.5
walkthrough.question_type: Fuel energy: heat, moles and mass
walkthrough.careful: Use |ΔHc| per mole; ΔH itself is not Q.
procedure: Write energy released = n × |ΔHc|.
Rearrange: n = energy ÷ |ΔHc|.
Convert moles to mass: m = n × M.
Check units: kJ with kJ, g with g mol−1.
tricks: 683.5 is half of 1367: half a mole, so 23 g.
Specific energy = |ΔHc| ÷ M in kJ g−1.
Unit-check each option: only one gives grams.
if_lost: How much energy does one mole of ethanol release?
What fraction of a mole releases 683.5 kJ?
How do you turn moles into grams?

1_context.short: AO2: link heat released to amount and mass of fuel.
1_context.why: R1.3.3 guidance covers energy released per unit mass. Exams run the calculation in either direction: mass to energy or energy to mass.
1_context.avoid: Treating ΔHc as the energy of the given mass.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.3.3: fuels compared by energy released per unit mass (guidance).
1_context.textbook_gap: Books measure ΔHc from experiment. Exams reverse it: energy needed to fuel mass, or fuel mass to water temperature rise.

2_markscheme_logic.short: C: heat over molar enthalpy, times M.
2_markscheme_logic.why: 683.5/1367 gives moles, and × 46.0 gives grams. Each distractor inverts one of these two ratios.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Using ΔH as Q, or fuel mass as m in mcΔT (25M.2.HL.6221.9 examiner).
trigger_phrases: Q = n × |ΔHc| then ΔT = Q / mc
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: 25M.2.HL.6221.9(c): marks lost for using ΔH as Q, 4.00 g as m, or no J/kJ conversion. ECF allowed from (b)(ii).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Right: (energy/|ΔHc|) × M. Tempting: inverting either ratio.

3_novel_application.short: Temperature rise of water heated by a fuel uses the same chain.
3_novel_application.avoid: Mixing specific energy (per mass) with energy density (per volume) (17M.3.HL.TZ2.17).
3_novel_application.disguise: ΔT of water heated by burning a fuel; specific energy or energy density of a fuel.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Fuel moles × |ΔHc| = Q = m(water) c ΔT. Per gram means specific energy; per dm3 means energy density.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ: choose the expression, no arithmetic needed.
4_command_terms.why: Only the structure of the expression is tested, so a unit check settles it faster than calculating.

5_time_efficiency.why: kJ ÷ kJ mol−1 × g mol−1 = g. Only C cancels to grams.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Calculating numerical values for each option.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 14 ΔHc ÷ M gives specific energy.
6_data_booklet.why: Section 14 gives ΔHc per mole. Hydrogen's −286 ÷ 2.02 ≈ 142 kJ g−1. Quoting 286 kJ g−1 was a reported error (17M.3.HL.TZ2.17).
6_data_booklet.avoid: Using the per-mole value as per-gram.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 14: ΔHc in kJ mol−1 (H2 −286, CH4 −891); divide by M for kJ g−1.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Specific energy = |ΔHc|/M and energy density are NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: A, B and D don't come out in grams.
7_elimination.why: Dimensional analysis needs no numbers. Only one arrangement turns kJ into g using kJ mol−1 and g mol−1.
7_elimination.avoid: Picking D because it 'uses both numbers'.

definitely_wrong.rule: Units are mol² g−1, not g.
Units are g−1; a mass can't come out this way.
Gives 92 g, two moles' mass for half a mole's energy.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.3.3: energy released per unit mass of fuel (guidance).
1_context.textbook_gap: Exams link fuel mass, ΔHc and the water's ΔT in one chain, and test specific energy against energy density.

trigger_phrases: kJ g−1 for specific energy, kJ dm−3 for energy density
trap_boundaries: ΔH used as Q, fuel mass as m, missing J/kJ conversion (25M.2.HL.6221.9).
Specific energy and energy density swapped; MJ/kJ errors cost a mark (17M.3.HL.TZ1.20).
A negative specific energy was marked wrong (24M.3.SL.TZ1.10).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial: right Q but wrong mass in mcΔT. Full: water mass, J and kJ consistent, positive ΔT.

disguises: ΔT of water from a fuel mass
Energy from 5.00 dm3 using energy density (20N.2.SL.TZ0.11)
Energy per mol from a 2-mol equation (09M.1.HL.TZ2.16)
3_novel_application.heuristic: Always reduce to moles of fuel × |ΔHc|, then convert.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Calculate: 1 mark per stage (Q, then ΔT). Comment: state a judgement, such as which fuel is better (17N.3.HL.TZ0.16).

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: In MCQs a dimension check replaces calculation.

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 14 ΔHc per mole ÷ M = specific energy. The definitions are NOT in the booklet.

rules: An expression that doesn't cancel to the asked unit is wrong.
Half the ΔHc energy means half a mole.
Specific energy and ΔT for heating are positive.

evidence.note: Mass of ethanol for 683.5 kJ = 683.5 × 46.0/1367; well answered.
Energy for 1 mol CO from a 2-mol equation: 282 kJ.
(c) Q = 119 kJ; ΔT = 56.9 K; ECF from (b)(ii) gives 52.5/52.6.
Errors: ΔH used as Q, 4.00 g used as m, missing unit conversion.
Many failed to calculate heat produced and temperature change.
Specific energy confused with energy density; 286 kJ g−1 cited for hydrogen.

cards.difficulty_signal: The MCQ form was well answered. The Paper 2 version (fuel to ΔT) was failed by many in 25M SL and HL; specific energy vs energy density is a recurring confusion.

cards.title: Spirit-burner calorimetry: heat loss hides in ΔT

walkthrough.question:
A spirit burner of ethanol heats a beaker of water from below, with a thermometer in the water. [Figure: burner with flame directly under the beaker; thermometer standing in the water.] Which quantity is likely to be the least accurate because of this set-up's sources of error?
A. Mass of ethanol burnt
B. Molecular mass of ethanol
C. Mass of water
D. Temperature change
walkthrough.key_idea: Heat escapes to air and beaker, so measured ΔT is too small.
walkthrough.careful: Heat loss makes ΔT and |ΔHc| too small.
procedure: Identify where heat goes besides the water.
List losses: air, beaker, incomplete combustion.
Find the reading that depends on heat received.
That reading (ΔT) carries the error; |ΔHc| comes out low.
tricks: Balance readings and Mr are precise; systematic heat loss hits ΔT.
Experimental |ΔHc| from a spirit burner is lower than the booklet value.
if_lost: Where does heat from the flame go besides the water?
Which reading would be smaller if heat escapes?
Which quantities come from a balance or a calculation?

1_context.short: AO3: judge which measurement the errors affect.
1_context.why: The guidance on energy per unit mass and incomplete combustion is tested through this classic practical. Examiners report weak experimental preparation.
1_context.avoid: Thinking every measurement is equally uncertain.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.3.3: energy released per unit mass; tendency for incomplete combustion (guidance).
1_context.textbook_gap: Books describe the method. Exams ask which reading carries the systematic error and in which direction.

2_markscheme_logic.short: D: temperature change is the least accurate.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Heat lost to the surroundings and to the beaker, plus incomplete combustion, means the water warms less. The error collects in ΔT.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Adding 273 to a temperature difference: 20% did (14M.1.SL.TZ2.16); converting 33.5 °C to K (12M.3.SL.TZ1.1).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: A ΔT in K equals the ΔT in °C: never add 273 to a difference.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Right: the systematic heat loss shows in ΔT. Tempting: a mass, measured precisely on a balance.

3_novel_application.short: Soot or a low ΔHc result: same heat-loss logic.
3_novel_application.why: Soot means incomplete combustion, so less energy is released (16N.3.SL.TZ0.2). Any energy not reaching the water shrinks ΔT and the calculated |ΔHc|.
3_novel_application.avoid: Blaming random error for a result that is always too low.
3_novel_application.disguise: Soot on the beaker, 'comment on the low value', or an improvement question.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Follow the heat. Anything that stops it reaching the water lowers ΔT.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ: one mark for the right reading.
4_command_terms.why: No calculation is needed. It's a judgement about where the systematic error sits.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the reading most affected by the errors.

5_time_efficiency.short: Follow the heat: 15 seconds, no numbers.
5_time_efficiency.why: Heat loss is the dominant error in this set-up. One question, 'which reading needs the heat?', gives the answer.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 14 values show how low your result is.
6_data_booklet.why: Comparing an experimental ΔHc with section 14 shows the size of the heat loss. The experimental magnitude is always smaller.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Expecting the booklet to list sources of error.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 14 ΔHc values (e.g. propan-1-ol −2021) as the reference for percentage error.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Sources of error and their direction are NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: B and C are not affected by heat loss.
7_elimination.why: Mr comes from atomic masses, not from the experiment. The water's mass is weighed once and does not change with heat loss.
7_elimination.avoid: Choosing C because water may evaporate slightly: it's a minor effect.

definitely_wrong.rule: Mr is calculated, not measured: no experimental error.
Balance reading of water is precise and not affected by heat loss.

walkthrough.answer: D. Heat lost to the air and beaker (and incomplete combustion) means the water warms less than it should, so ΔT is the least accurate.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.3.3: energy per unit mass; incomplete combustion.
1_context.textbook_gap: Exams test the practical's systematic errors and unit handling, not just the method.

trap_boundaries: Adding 273 to ΔT (14M.1.SL.TZ2.16).
J vs kJ mix-ups and a missing negative sign for ΔH (12M.3.SL.TZ1.1, 16M.2.SL.TZ0.2).
A negative ΔT when the water is heated (16M.2.SL.TZ0.2).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial: names an error. Full: names the error and how it changes ΔT and ΔHc.

disguises: Soot on glassware
Low experimental ΔHc to comment on
Which change improves accuracy
3_novel_application.heuristic: Follow the heat. Losses lower ΔT and |ΔHc|.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark per error with its effect. 'Comment' needs a clear judgement (17N.3.HL.TZ0.16).

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip calculations when only the error source is asked.

6_data_booklet.hack: Compare the experimental ΔHc with section 14 to judge heat loss. Error analysis is NOT in the booklet.

rules: Calculated quantities (Mr) carry no experimental error.
Balance masses are rarely the main error in combustion calorimetry.
A heat-loss error always makes |ΔHc| smaller, never larger.

evidence.note: Spirit burner: temperature change is the least accurate quantity.
Nearly 20% added 273 to a temperature difference.
°C converted to K wrongly, J/kJ errors, negative sign omitted.
J vs kJ confusion and negative ΔT for heated air.
